chunks: Amir Al-Momineen (peace be upon him) said: 'Neither a man nor a woman shall be stoned until four witnesses testify against him/her upon the penetration and the withdrawal.'

key_terms.أَرْبَعَةُ شُهُودٍ: arba'a shuhud — four witnesses, the minimum number required for establishing hadd punishments
key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Amir Al-Momineen — Commander of the Believers, the title of Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (AS)
key_terms.الْإِخْرَاجِ: al-ikhraj — the act of withdrawal, the second element witnesses must directly observe
key_terms.الْإِيلَاجِ: al-ilaj — the act of penetration, one of the two elements witnesses must directly observe
key_terms.يُرْجَمُ: rajm — the hadd punishment of stoning to death, prescribed for proven adultery (zina) in Islamic law

ai.seo_question: How many witnesses are required for stoning in Islamic law according to Imam Ali?
ai.summary: This hadith records a ruling of Imam Ali (AS), Amir Al-Momineen, transmitted through Imam al-Baqir (AS), establishing that the hadd punishment of stoning (rajm) for adultery cannot be applied unless four witnesses directly observe both the act of penetration and withdrawal. This extraordinarily high evidentiary threshold — four eyewitnesses to the most intimate act — reflects the Islamic legal tradition's prioritization of protecting individuals from false accusations over punishing sins. In classical Shia jurisprudence, this requirement effectively makes stoning nearly impossible to execute through testimonial evidence alone, with jurists noting that the primary purpose of the rule is deterrence and the preservation of public morality.
